title: An alphabet of wisdom
hook: tradition sets it at Onkareshwar, where Nanak answered a pandit with a poem on the letters

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sidh Gosht close: a conversation with other seekers, kept as scripture. Your line was keep talking. Did you ask your real question? Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

A, apple. B, ball. C, cat. Somewhere, a child is chanting letters right now, pointing at a picture for each one. Alphabets often get taught that way: a sound, a shape, a thing to hang it on. Tradition tells of Guru Nanak coming to Onkareshwar, a temple town on a river, and meeting a pandit there, a learned teacher of scripture and letters. Nanak answered him with a poem that walks through the letters one by one. But the picture hung on each letter isn't an apple or a ball. Today: an alphabet of wisdom. Its name is Oankar.
screen: `A, APPLE. B, BALL.` → `A PANDIT AT ONKARESHWAR.` → `A POEM ON THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The poem sits in Raga Ramkali, just before the Sidh Gosht we've been reading. Its heading calls it Dakhni Oankar, Oankar of the south, which fits the tradition that places it at a temple to the south of the Punjab. Oankar is a name for the One: the sound that stands at the head of the Guru Granth Sahib itself, in the symbol Ik Oankar, One Creator. So the poem's title is also its subject. Here's how it works. In the story, the pandit is a kind of gatekeeper: learn the letters, and the scriptures open. Nanak keeps the gate and changes what's behind it. In the poem, a letter is named, and then, instead of a word to spell, comes a teaching about the One, about the mind, about how to live. The alphabet becomes a ladder of wisdom. That isn't an attack on learning. Guru Nanak honored letters. In the Japji he says, in paraphrase: through letters we speak the Name, through letters we praise; through letters come knowledge and song; through letters things are written and spoken. Letters are a gift. The question the Oankar asks is what we do with them. Spell our way to arguments, or let each letter point somewhere true. And there's something tender in the choice of form. An alphabet is something a child learns early, an ordinary schoolroom thing. Nanak meets a scholar with the simplest tool in the room and fills it to the brim. Over the next days we'll read pieces of it. Today, just the shape: letters, each one carrying wisdom.
screen: `DAKHNI OANKAR: OANKAR OF THE SOUTH.` · `OANKAR: A NAME FOR THE ONE.` · `THROUGH LETTERS WE PRAISE.` · `EACH LETTER CARRIES WISDOM.` · then, large: `LETTERS OF WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one letter. The poem's name begins with the Gurmukhi sound o, written ਓ. If you have a screen nearby, look at it for a moment, then close your eyes and trace its shape in the air with one finger, slowly, the way a child would. Say the sound softly: o. If you already read Gurmukhi, choose a letter you love instead, and let it carry one thing you know about the One. If you pray, you can let the letter become a short prayer of attention. If you don't, just stay with the shape and the sound. The bell holds the time.
Oankar. A name for the One, and the title of Guru Nanak's poem on the letters, answered, tradition says, to a pandit at Onkareshwar. Today's word.
Your line: letters of wisdom. Today, when you write something, a text, a list, a note, choose one word in it on purpose, and let it carry something good. Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: The Oankar, Guru Nanak's poem on the letters, is in Raga Ramkali in the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikh children learning Gurmukhi are often taught that the script carries the Guru's Word.
